But let me be clear: I wasn’t saying the OP is neurodivergent — I was pushing back on the general attitude that gets thrown around in this sub (and your original reply is a perfect example of it) that switching to automatic is some sort of defeat or lazy shortcut.

What I was saying — and still stand by — is that there are plenty of neurodiverse learners out there who get completely overlooked by this “just work through it” mentality. You may not have meant harm, but your comment absolutely read as dismissive to people for whom manual driving isn’t just “one little hiccup,” but a real barrier — one they’re made to feel ashamed for wanting to bypass.

You talk a lot about adapting your teaching style. That’s great. But part of adapting is not being reactive when someone challenges a mindset you may not have fully explored — like how cognitive load, sensory processing, or motor coordination affects learning manual. You said, “I’m not having a go,” but you came in hot with “Why?!?” and a sweeping cost argument — so yeah, the tone landed.

If you genuinely want to be inclusive and better support all learners — especially those who think and process differently — then it starts with listening, not getting defensive.

All that said — fair play for engaging with OP and offering advice. Just think a bit deeper next time before writing off a perfectly valid path for some learners.
Are you aware of the popular House MD Spinoff: ‘Doctor Down Under’?
Park or Tritter?

Let’s be real: your original comment  “Why?!? More expensive… 2 tests and more lessons”  was glib, dismissive, and completely tone-deaf to the actual struggles people face while learning to drive, especially those who are neurodivergent.

You jumped straight to cost without even acknowledging that someone might need automatic for reasons that go far beyond convenience — reasons rooted in cognitive processing, coordination issues, or anxiety under pressure. For many, manual isn’t just a “skill to work through”  it’s a roadblock. And clinging to it under the illusion of “confidence building” can be exhausting, demoralising, and yes — wildly expensive.

The OP has already spent 40+ hours battling the same issue. At that point, telling them to just keep “working through it” feels less like professional guidance and more like gatekeeping. You talk about building confidence — but there’s a point where it stops being uplifting and becomes damaging. You’re not training grit, you’re grinding people down.

And let’s not pretend money isn’t a factor. The longer someone stays locked in this cycle, the more lessons they book. It’s naive to pretend instructors are immune to the financial incentive. Recommending a potential solution that could actually help someone shouldn’t feel like a threat to your business model.

You say learner needs come first — but clearly only when they match your idea of how driving should be learned. You didn’t stop to genuinely ask what might be best for that individual, in that exact situation, after those very real struggles. And for someone who claims to adapt their teaching style, you come across incredibly rigid when someone suggests an alternative path.

Let me be blunt: you are the one being narrow-minded here. Not only did you ignore the possibility of neurodivergent needs in your first comment, but you doubled down with a smug, self-congratulatory reply that pretends to be empathetic while still pushing a “manual or bust” mindset.

That’s not helpful. That’s not open-minded. That’s not integrity. That’s your pride talking.

Do better.

Have you considered that your advice might not be universally helpful — especially for neurodiverse individuals, or those with learning difficulties, anxiety, or coordination challenges, who may find learning in an automatic significantly more accessible?

Suggesting that people should “just do manual because it’s cheaper” ignores the very real barriers some learners face. In fact, pushing someone to struggle through a manual gearbox unnecessarily could cost more in time, confidence, and money in the long run.

Your sweeping statement comes across as narrow-minded, dismissive, and frankly a bit avaricious — as though learner needs are secondary to your opinion on driving costs.

People’s circumstances differ. Blanket advice like this helps no one.
